entries.title: Bulls' offense won't change without Caleb Wilson
entries.summary: <p>With one win in the Bulls’ first 10 games, fans were coming to grips with the idea that this season would be about Caleb Wilson’s development and his pursuit of the NBA Rookie of the Year award.</p><p>Both are on hold after Wilson, the fourth overall pick in the draft, had surgery Thursday for a broken right hand he suffered Wednesday against the Spurs. For at least a month, fans will have to put their focus on something else — and that won’t be easy on this team.</p><p>Wilson entered the game Friday against the Hawks as the Bulls’ second-leading scorer, averaging 18.9 points, just behind team leader Norman Powell (19.3). Among rookies, Wilson was third in scoring, first in steals per game (1.8) and second in blocked shots (0.9). He was among the early leaders for the top rookie honor.</p><p>“To see a guy that’s just come in, he’s played 10 games in the NBA, he’s playing really well and then to get injured like that, it sucks,” Josh Giddey said.</p><p>“He’s frustrated, just like all of us,” coach Tiago Splitter said.</p><p>Wilson has been unlucky with his hand health. At North Carolina, he broke his left hand in February, and after being cleared to work out, he broke his right thumb on a dunk in March. It’s widely believed that had Wilson not gotten hurt, he wouldn’t have fallen to the Bulls.</p><p>That’s one break that went the Bulls’ way. Splitter said he asked Wilson about his rash of hand injuries.</p><p>“It’s just bad luck, a freak injury,” Splitter said. “Just have to be patient.”</p><p>The Bulls hadn’t been so patient on the court with Wilson. They had been throwing a lot at him, and he had been responding with not just numbers but development. He also had been jelling with his teammates in Splitter’s uptempo offense.</p><p>Now that offense, which finally has been working as it's supposed to — better shooting certainly has helped — is without a key cog. But Splitter said he won’t change the offense, though others will have to make up for the team-high 16 shots Wilson took per game.</p><p>“Of course, we’re going to miss him, but it doesn’t change what we want to do,” Splitter said. “Everybody else is going to have more shots. I don’t expect just one guy to be more aggressive. Naturally, the game’s going to find the shots, and the players are going to take those shots. I’m not worried about that.”</p><p>“It’s a big hole to fill,” Giddey said. “He was very productive for us on both sides of the ball. I don’t think it’s as simple as just putting someone in to replace Caleb. It’s going to have to be by committee. It allows opportunities for other guys to come in and play a bigger role.”</p><p>Two of those players will be big men Nic Claxton and Jalen Smith, who Splitter said will see more time together now that Claxton is closer to playing normal minutes. He was restricted to about 16-20 minutes in his first two games back from a hamstring injury that cost him a month. Splitter said the team wants him to play about 20-24 minutes.</p><p>Fortunately for the Bulls, Powell returned from back spasms that kept him out of two games. The veteran guard entered the game averaging the second-most shots on the team with 13, though he had made only 40% of them, 70 points below his career average.</p><p>As for Wilson, Splitter said he’ll stay involved with the team, being at practice and watching video. Splitter said that was important for Wilson, as well as seeing the game from a different perspective. With a hand injury, he’ll be able to stay in shape, though not exactly game shape. Splitter had an idea interesting idea for Wilson.</p><p>“Maybe work on the left hook or something like that,” he said.</p>

entries.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop. O'Hare, Midway flights can resume after hours of delays, cancellations
entries.summary: <p>Hours after the Federal Aviation Administration halted flights across the country Friday, including at Midway and O'Hare airports, the agency said departures can resume.</p><p>Officials blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system" for instability in air traffic control communications during a White House briefing Friday evening.</p><p>Inside O’Hare International Airport — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/20/ohare-reclaims-top-spot-named-nations-busiest-airport-in-2025" target="_blank" >the busiest airport in the U.S.</a> — confused passengers wandered around as luggage piled up on baggage carousels. Long lines of travelers rummaged through hundreds of bags from flights that never took off because of the delay.</p><p>The FAA grounded all flights nationwide at around 2:36 p.m., and an FAA alert said the stoppage was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." They said they lifted the ground stop at 7:15 p.m., though it was unclear when flights actually would resume.</p><p>A sudden silence fell over O'Hare as travelers were notified that the ground stop had been lifted. But a video board displaying flight information still showed delays or cancellations even though many passengers attempted to buy tickets at nearby airline kiosks. </p><p>"For an 18-hour trip back and forth, it doesn't make sense for us and try to go," said Angelica Colmenares, who was en route to Paris for a 48-hour trip with a friend. Luckily, we were flying standby so we didn't fly, but now we're going to have our own party in Chicago."</p><p>Some airlines, including JetBlue and Air Canada, had already said they were canceling the rest of their Friday night flights.</p><p>U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the public was "never in danger" and the flights were grounded due to an "abundance of caution."</p><p>By 5:30 p.m., O'Hare had reported 328 flight cancellations and 847 delays. Midway saw 30 canceled flights and 186 delays, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.flychicago.com/business/media/delays/pages/default.aspx" target="_blank" >Chicago Department of Aviation</a>. </p><p>As of 6:15 p.m. on Friday, 30 flights scheduled to arrive at O'Hare since 2:55 p.m. had been diverted. Ten arrivals scheduled at Midway were also diverted. </p><p>U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communication issue affected all of the nation's 22 air traffic control centers that route planes between airports.</p><p>During the evening briefing, Duffy shifted focus to a political fight, saying the Trump administration had been “asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system.”</p><p>Mullin said there was no sign yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage."</p><p>“Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying,” he said.</p><p>Although the order was lifted, Duffy said he expected it to take a bit to catch up on flight schedules. “Hopefully tomorrow, we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said.</p><p>Earlier at O'Hare, video boards displaying flight information were checkered with red and yellow, signifying the delays and cancellations that forced many travelers to book hotel rooms for the night or rent a car to arrive at their destinations.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div across the country. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Prospect Heights residents Matt and Patricia Kowalski arrived at O’Hare two hours early for their annual holiday trip to visit family in Poland, prepared to board a flight to Germany.</p><p>Matt Kowalski learned through the radio on their ride to the airport that a ground stop had occurred, so they decided to wait it out.</p><p>By 5 p.m., they had already missed their connecting flight and were debating waiting another three investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.</p><p>The FAA, in a separate statement, said the ground stop was issued "out of an abundance of caution. "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis," the FAA said.</p><p>Nashville resident Paul Lindsay, who was at O'Hare, was on his way to Mason City, Iowa, with friends.</p><p>"This is nuts," he said. "It's good to know this is not our problem. Every person in an airport in the United States is running into this problem."</p><p>The Chicago Department of Aviation said it had no comment and directed questions to the FAA.</p><p>U.S. Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, called for more congressional oversight of the FAA and air traffic control in a statement Friday evening.</p><p>“My team and I are monitoring the nationwide ground stop that the FAA has ordered, which is causing major travel disruptions and affecting millions nationwide," the statement said. "... I will demand answers from the FAA; Congress must be briefed, and there must be a thorough investigation into the cause of this massive disruption to our aviation system.”</p><div class="Enhancement" Check back for updates.</i></p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press</i></p>

entries.title: CPS faces possible midyear budget cuts as unexpected funding costs mount
entries.summary: <p>Just a few months into the school year, Chicago Public Schools has overspent its budget and its emergency contingency budget for special education by $27 million — one of several “compounding financial pressures” that could mean midyear cuts if the school district doesn’t get more from the state in the state Legislative veto session that starts Tuesday.</p><p>Besides ballooning special education costs, CPS officials say they had to pay more than expected in interest on short-term loans to make payroll and received $19 million less in state funding than expected.</p><p>And these unexpected costs don’t even include the staff that CPS rehired this fall at the direction of school board members aligned with the Chicago Teachers Union. In a controversial move, these members approved a last-minute budget amendment counting on $150 million more from the state, even though it had yet to be committed.</p><p>The district only wound up re-hiring some of the staff laid off — 128 teachers and 153 support staff at a cost of $29 million. District officials are already planning to re-lay off those staff members as early as Dec. 1 if no additional money comes through, according to a memo obtained by the Chicago Tribune.</p><p>But district officials have yet to say how they plan to handle the other costs that are creating a hole in the district’s budget.</p><p>“The CPS Finance team is closely monitoring our budget, assessing implications of rising costs and a shortfall if no additional state revenue is received, and identifying potential solutions,” CPS officials said in a statement. “CPS will continue to keep our Board and community apprised of any additional financial savings that will need to be enacted this school year.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> on the city pulling $285 million out of special taxing districts called TIFs and sending it to the school district. Mayor Brandon Johnson’s budget provides this revenue, but it has yet to be approved by the City Council, some of whose members have balked at the amount.</p><p>The CTU, in a message sent to its members on Friday, said laying off staff would create chaos and pointed out that rehiring staff turns out not to be the most urgent financial problem facing the district.</p><p>“Before CPS reversed one layoff at the beginning of the school year, the district was already coming up short because of the Governor and the Illinois General Assembly’s skipping its payments to Chicago and other districts across the state,” CTU leaders told members, referring to the fact that the state doesn’t provide the funding that it says CPS needs to provide an adequate education to students.</p><p>CPS leaders and board members, along with groups of members from CTU and other major CPS unions are planning to go to Springfield for the veto session to lobby for more money.</p><p>Still, many have said that the chances that CPS gets additional funding from the state is unlikely. House Speaker Chris Welch said this summer that he was open to it, but he will be a lame duck during the veto session, as he’s decided not to run for his leadership position. And Gov. Fowler/The State Journal-Register via AP)<br></p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Chicago isn’t the only school district hoping for more money.</p><p>The Illinois Federation of Teachers this month called on lawmakers to provide an additional $670 million towards education funding during the veto session, $400 million of which would go towards the state's general education funding and $100 million for services the state requires, such as transportation.</p><p>Those funds wouldn’t close the funding gap that exists statewide but would provide “urgently needed relief and help,” said Arnoldo Fabela, IFT director of field and organizing. In 2017, Illinois changed the way it distributed funds to school districts. The law established the amount of funding each district needs to provide an adequate education. Illinois has fallen way behind on meeting those targets.</p><p>Of about 940 school districts, 714 have moved further away from adequacy this school year. That’s despite education funding in Illinois rising overall under Pritzker. In Chicago, CPS now has only 70% of what it needs to provide an adequate education, down from 73% last year and 79% the year before.</p><p>Many factors are causing the state to fall short, including a change in the way the state counts the number of poor students and costs going up.</p><p>Any state funding package would likely need to include much more than what CPS needs and money for other underfunded districts in order to get any traction, making it a costly proposition. That means district leaders will have to get legislators from outside of Chicago on board with their plan. Some have expressed skepticism about giving schools in Chicago more money.</p><p><i>Sarah Karp covers education for WBEZ.
